title: Stash & Reset
subtitle: Save work temporarily and undo changes
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: You have half-finished work when an urgent bug arrives. Or you committed something wrong and need to undo it. You need ways to save work-in-progress and reverse mistakes.
whyItExists.solution: git stash saves your uncommitted changes aside. git reset moves the branch pointer backward to undo commits. git restore discards changes in individual files.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Stash when switching contexts mid-work. Reset to undo recent commits (locally). Restore to discard file changes.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't reset commits you've already pushed to a shared branch. Use git revert instead — it adds a new commit that undoes the change.

explainModes.beginner: git stash is like a clipboard for your uncommitted changes — save them now, come back later. git reset lets you undo commits by moving the branch back in time. git restore throws away changes to a specific file.
explainModes.simple: git stash — saves staged and unstaged changes. git stash pop — restores them. git reset --soft HEAD~1 — undoes last commit but keeps changes staged. git reset --hard HEAD~1 — undoes last commit and DISCARDS changes. git restore file.html — discards file's changes (unrecoverable).
explainModes.standard: Reset modes: --soft moves HEAD only (changes stay staged). --mixed (default) moves HEAD and clears staging (changes stay in working tree). --hard moves HEAD and clears both staging and working tree — changes are gone. Stash saves to a stack — git stash list shows all entries. git stash apply leaves the stash entry; git stash pop removes it.
explainModes.technical: git stash creates two commits: one for the index and one for the working tree, referenced as stash@{0}. git stash --include-untracked stashes new untracked files too. git stash branch feature/name creates a new branch from the stash. git reset moves HEAD (and the branch ref it points to) — it does NOT move the stash. git reflog lets you recover from accidental --hard resets by finding the old HEAD hash.
explainModes.deepDive: git reset --hard is recoverable for about 30 days via git reflog, because Git's garbage collector doesn't immediately delete unreachable objects. git clean -fd removes untracked files (irreversible, not stashed). git restore --source=HEAD~2 file.txt restores a file to its state 2 commits ago without resetting the branch. git revert <hash> is the safe alternative to reset for pushed commits — it creates a new commit that undoes the changes.

content.code:
# You have uncommitted changes but need to switch branches
git stash
# → Saved working directory and index state

# Give your stash a name (recommended)
git stash push -m "half-finished login form"

# List all stashed items
git stash list
# → stash@{0}: On feature: half-finished login form
# → stash@{1}: WIP on main: a3b2c1d Update footer

# Restore most recent stash (and remove from stack)
git stash pop

# Restore a specific stash entry (keep in stack)
git stash apply stash@{1}

# Drop a specific entry
git stash drop stash@{1}

# Include new untracked files in the stash
git stash --include-untracked

# --soft: undo commit, keep changes STAGED
git reset --soft HEAD~1
# Useful: fix the commit message or add a forgotten file

# --mixed (default): undo commit, keep changes in working tree (unstaged)
git reset HEAD~1
# Useful: split a commit into smaller ones

# --hard: undo commit AND discard all changes (DESTRUCTIVE!)
git reset --hard HEAD~1
# ⚠️ Changes are gone. Only safe if you haven't pushed.

# Recover from --hard with reflog
git reflog
# → a3b2c1d HEAD@{1}: commit: Add login form  ← find this hash
git reset --hard a3b2c1d   # go back to it

# Discard unstaged changes in a file (UNRECOVERABLE)
git restore index.html

# Unstage a file (keep changes in working tree)
git restore --staged index.html

# Restore a file to its state 2 commits ago
git restore --source=HEAD~2 index.html

# For pushed commits — use revert instead of reset!
git revert HEAD        # creates a new commit undoing the last one
git revert a3b2c1d     # reverts a specific commit

content.text: git reset --hard and git restore can permanently discard work. Always check git status before using them. For pushed commits, use git revert instead — it's reversible.

questions.question: What is the difference between git stash pop and git stash apply?
options: pop is faster; apply is safer
pop restores and removes the stash entry; apply restores but keeps it in the stack
apply only works for staged files; pop works for everything
questions.explanation: git stash pop restores the stash and removes it from the stack (like 'pop' in a stack data structure). git stash apply restores the stash but leaves the entry in the stack so you can apply it again or to another branch.

faq.q: I did git reset --hard and lost changes. Can I recover them?
faq.a: Maybe. Run git reflog to find the SHA of the commit before the reset. Then git reset --hard <that-sha> to go back. This works as long as Git's garbage collector hasn't run (usually 30+ days). git fsck --lost-found can also find dangling objects.

faq.q: What is git revert and when should I use it instead of reset?
faq.a: git revert <hash> creates a new commit that undoes the changes of the specified commit — it does NOT rewrite history. Use it whenever the commit you want to undo has been pushed to a shared branch. Reset is for local-only history; revert is for shared history.

examples: git stash → git switch main → fix bug → git switch feature → git stash pop
git reset --soft HEAD~1 to re-commit with a better message before pushing
git revert HEAD on main after discovering a broken deployment
